title: K-prop: Deep Online Learning by Backpropagating Temporal Kernels
summary: Self-recurrence represents an important component for temporal processing in neural networks, both artificial and biological, where it appears naturally in the form of leaky integration. However, due to the complex temporal dependencies of the gradient, an efficient and effective method of online training is still lacking. Here we propose K-prop, a novel online learning method for leaky neural networks. It dramatically reduces the computational and memory cost of real time recurrent learning (RTRL) by propagating kernel gains. K-prop also outperforms existing RTRL approximations and achieves performance comparable to backpropagation through time in sequence learning, classification, and reinforcement learning tasks. We further analyze how its sole approximation affects gradient quality and identify conditions under which K-prop remains accurate and effective.
core_methodology: K-prop is an online learning method for leaky neural networks that reduces computational and memory costs of real-time recurrent learning (RTRL) by propagating kernel gains. It achieves performance comparable to backpropagation through time in sequence learning, classification, and reinforcement learning tasks.
data_sources: Not specified in the abstract, but typically applicable to time-series data which could include financial market data.
alpha_potential: Potential for improving real-time trading strategies that rely on temporal data processing, such as high-frequency trading or algorithmic execution, by enabling more efficient online learning of temporal dependencies.
title_cn: K-prop：通过反向传播时间核进行深度在线学习

title: Simulation-aided Reinforcement Learning with Control Variates
summary: Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms often rely on data collected from a target environment, which can be expensive and noisy. Although simulators can generate large amounts of additional data, standard simulation mixing approaches, which directly combine simulated and real experience, can degrade performance due to simulator inaccuracies, especially when they bias the solution away from the optimal policy. We propose a conservative simulation-aided learning method based on control variates, where simulated data is used solely to reduce variance in the learning process rather than directly shaping the learning target. We develop our approach for Policy-Evaluation, which is a fundamental building block of RL algorithms. Then we combine it within the actor-critic framework towards policy improvement, as well as extend it towards offline RL scenarios. Experiments on multiple MuJoCo benchmark tasks demonstrate improvements over standard simulation mixing approaches, highlighting control variates as an effective tool for simulation-aided reinforcement learning.
core_methodology: The paper introduces a conservative simulation-aided learning method based on control variates, specifically for Policy-Evaluation in Reinforcement Learning (RL). It aims to reduce variance in the learning process by using simulated data without letting simulator inaccuracies bias the optimal policy. The approach is extended within the actor-critic framework and adapted for offline RL scenarios.
data_sources: The methodology is tested on MuJoCo benchmark tasks, which are standard in RL research but not directly related to financial data. However, the approach is generic and could be adapted to high-frequency or algorithmic trading contexts where simulation data (e.g., synthetic market data) is used alongside real market data.
alpha_potential: The primary alpha potential lies in the method's ability to improve the robustness of RL-based trading strategies by leveraging simulated data to reduce variance without introducing bias. This could be particularly useful in environments where real data is expensive or noisy, such as in high-frequency trading or complex derivatives markets.

title: Vendi Anomaly Scores for Efficient and Accurate Anomaly Detection
summary: Anomaly detection (AD) is a critical for trustworthy machine learning and scientific discovery. Existing methods typically define anomalies through local density, isolation heuristics, or distance from a fitted distribution, making them sensitive to neighborhood scale, partitioning choices, or restrictive distributional assumptions. In this work, we introduce a new paradigm by formulating anomaly detection from a diversity perspective. We propose the $\textit{Vendi Anomaly Score}$ (VAS), which detects anomalies by quantifying how much a sample changes the diversity of the dataset, as measured by the Vendi score, when removed. VAS captures both local redundancy and global data structure without relying on density estimation or partitioning heuristics. Moreover, VAS requires no hyperparameter tuning, instead adapting automatically to the spectral structure of the data. VAS is non-parametric and scales linearly with dataset size. Across 148 benchmark embedding datasets derived from 10 source datasets and 4 embedding architectures, VAS achieves state-of-the-art AD performance. We further validate VAS on large-scale ImageNet experiments, where it remains robust as both contamination rate and dataset scale increase.
core_methodology: The paper introduces the Vendi Anomaly Score (VAS), a novel anomaly detection method that quantifies how much a sample changes the diversity of the dataset when removed. It leverages the Vendi score to measure diversity, capturing both local redundancy and global data structure without relying on density estimation or partitioning heuristics. The method is non-parametric, scales linearly with dataset size, and requires no hyperparameter tuning.
data_sources: The paper evaluates VAS on 148 benchmark embedding datasets derived from 10 source datasets and 4 embedding architectures, as well as large-scale ImageNet experiments. While not financial data, the methodology is generalizable to financial time series or alternative data embeddings.
alpha_potential: VAS could be adapted to detect anomalies in financial time series, such as unusual price movements, liquidity shocks, or structural breaks in market regimes. Its ability to capture both local and global structure without restrictive assumptions makes it potentially useful for identifying rare events or regime changes that could inform trading strategies.

title: Information-Theoretic Generalization for Set-Input Optimization-Valued Objectives
summary: Modern machine learning is increasingly evaluated using criteria such as multicalibration, CVaR, and Cressie-Read DRO, which target subgroup reliability, tail risk, and distributional robustness rather than averages of fixed per-example losses. Existing information-theoretic generalization bounds for pointwise losses do not directly apply, because these empirical criteria depend on the entire batch and involve a post-hoc auxiliary optimization over witnesses, thresholds, or reweightings. We formalize this structure as set-input optimization-valued objectives. In the balanced supersample setting, we bound the expected optimized validation-training gap in terms of an objective-dependent sub-Gaussian parameter and the square root of the prediction-based conditional mutual information (fCMI) between the learned supersample prediction table and the selector vector. Combining this with fixed-predictor population-validation comparisons yields unified algorithm-dependent generalization bounds. We verify sub-Gaussianity of the selector gap using stability and convex L2-Lipschitz certificates, obtaining concrete bounds for multicalibration, CVaR, and Cressie-Read DRO, with a stability-based single-index refinement.
core_methodology: The paper introduces set-input optimization-valued objectives to generalize machine learning evaluation criteria like multicalibration, CVaR, and Cressie-Read DRO, focusing on subgroup reliability, tail risk, and distributional robustness. It provides information-theoretic generalization bounds using concepts like fCMI and objective-dependent sub-Gaussian parameters.
data_sources: Theoretical framework applicable to any batch data, but specific examples include financial datasets where tail risk (CVaR) and distributional robustness are critical.
alpha_potential: Potential application in risk management and robust portfolio optimization, particularly in strategies that require tail risk control (e.g., CVaR-based portfolio construction) or distributionally robust optimization (DRO) for market regimes.

title: Zeroth-Order Langevin Dynamics for Stochastic Nonconvex Optimization: Curvature Regularization and Non-Asymptotic Guarantees
summary: Zeroth-order methods provide a way to optimize stochastic nonconvex objectives using only noisy function evaluations. However, the smoothing inherent in their gradient estimators effectively modifies the objective being optimized. In particular, Gaussian smoothing with smoothing parameter $\eta>0$ induces, to leading order, an implicit Hessian-trace regularization, which motivates the study of the curvature-regularized objective of the form $f(x)+(\eta^2/2) tr(\nabla^2 f(x))$. We develop a non-asymptotic theory in the nonconvex setting for a class of algorithms called stochastic zeroth-order Langevin dynamics (ZOLD), which use only noisy function evaluations and do not have access to first- or higher-order derivative information, and derive excess-risk guarantees for the curvature-regularized objective. We first control the finite-time distribution of the ZOLD iterates in Wasserstein distance with respect to the Gibbs measure associated with the Gaussian-smoothed objective. An explicit coupling between the smoothing and inverse temperature parameters then quantifies the proximity of this measure to the Gibbs measure associated with the corresponding Hessian-trace-regularized objective. These distributional estimates in Wasserstein distance lead to excess-risk bounds for the curvature-regularized objective. Our analysis accommodates assumptions under which the stochastic function evaluations are allowed to have non-uniform dependence on the data stream. In addition, the constants in the non-asymptotic bounds do not rely on log-Sobolev or Poincar\'e inequalities as in prior zeroth-order Langevin analyses. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first non-asymptotic analysis of a zeroth-order Langevin method that simultaneously establishes excess-risk guarantees for a curvature-regularized objective and Wasserstein guarantees for the associated Gibbs measure in the nonconvex setting.
core_methodology: Stochastic zeroth-order Langevin dynamics (ZOLD) for optimizing nonconvex objectives using only noisy function evaluations, with Hessian-trace regularization
data_sources: No specific financial data sources mentioned, but methodology could be applied to noisy financial time series or other irregular financial data
alpha_potential: Potential application in optimization of complex trading cost functions or non-standard objective functions where gradient information is unavailable

title: Deep backward multistep high-order regression methods for high dimensional nonlinear parabolic partial differential equations
summary: We propose a deep backward multistep high-order regression (MHDBR) method for semilinear parabolic partial differential equations through their backward stochastic differential equation representations. The method combines multistep time discretization with regression targets formed by conditional expectations. Under explicit regularity, starting-value, forward-approximation and network-moment assumptions, we prove an error bound separating time discretization, conditional Monte Carlo sampling and neural-network approximation. The analysis assumes exact population minimization; finite-training-sample generalization and optimization errors are not included. For generators independent of the gradient variable, suitably constrained GroupSort networks and sufficiently large conditional sample sizes give order $J$ in the stated nodal $L^2$ error norm. The required network sizes depend on dimension, so this result does not establish dimension-independent complexity. We present a reproducible time-discretization test satisfying the analytical assumptions and three broader neural-network benchmarks, whose relation to the assumptions is discussed explicitly.
core_methodology: The paper proposes a deep learning method (MHDBR) for solving high-dimensional nonlinear parabolic PDEs through backward stochastic differential equations, combining multistep time discretization with neural network-based regression of conditional expectations.
data_sources: Theoretical framework applicable to financial derivatives pricing where underlying assets follow diffusion processes (no specific market data mentioned).
alpha_potential: Potential applications in derivatives pricing and hedging for complex financial instruments where traditional PDE solvers struggle with high dimensionality, though practical implementation challenges remain.
