Second, LiSSA iterations are destabilized by negative Hessian eigenvalues, which existing methods handle via $\ell_2$ damping, at the cost of a biased inverse-Hessian-vector product (iHVP) estimate. p-LiSSA eliminates this bias by solving the restricted inverse-Hessian problem without such damping. We further show that the presence of low-curvature directions slows p-LiSSA convergence, and that the data-relevant subspace selected by GIFs mitigates this. Across five image and text unlearning benchmarks, GIFs update only 10% of the parameters yet preserve accuracy up to 2.12 percentage points better than IF-based baselines, while improving unlearning performance by up to 2.73 percentage points. Moreover, p-LiSSA improves restricted iHVP estimation by reducing the residual by 9.6$\times$ over existing iHVP baselines, while using 19.8% less memory with comparable computation time. Code is available at https://github.com/hslyu/GIF.
core_methodology: Generalized influence functions (GIFs) and pseudo-LiSSA (p-LiSSA) for more accurate model editing by restricting updates to data-relevant subspaces and improving inverse-Hessian-vector product estimation
data_sources: Image and text datasets (non-financial)
alpha_potential: Potential for improving model robustness in financial ML applications, but requires adaptation to market data contexts

title: Partially Decentralized Multi-Agent Q-Learning via Digital Cousins for Wireless Networks
summary: Q-learning is a widely used reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm for optimizing wireless networks, but faces challenges with large state-spaces. Recently proposed multi-environment mixed Q-learning (MEMQ) algorithm addresses these challenges by employing multiple Q-learning algorithms across multiple synthetically generated, distinct but structurally related environments, so-called digital cousins. In this paper, we propose a novel multi-agent MEMQ (M-MEMQ) for cooperative decentralized wireless networks with multiple networked transmitters (TXs) and base stations (BSs). TXs do not have access to global information (joint state and actions). The new concept of coordinated and uncoordinated states is introduced. In uncoordinated states, TXs act independently to minimize their individual costs and update local Q-functions. In coordinated states, TXs use a Bayesian approach to estimate the joint state and update the joint Q-functions. The cost of information-sharing scales linearly with the number of TXs and is independent of the joint state-action space size. Several theoretical guarantees, including deterministic and probabilistic convergence, bounds on estimation error variance, and the probability of misdetecting the joint states, are given. Numerical simulations show that M-MEMQ outperforms several decentralized and centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE) multi-agent RL algorithms by achieving 60% lower average policy error (APE), 40% faster convergence, 45% reduced runtime complexity, and 40% less sample complexity. Furthermore, M-MEMQ achieves comparable APE with significantly lower complexity than centralized methods. Simulations validate the theoretical analyses.
core_methodology: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) with partial decentralization via digital cousins, employing both coordinated and uncoordinated states for decision-making.
data_sources: Simulated wireless network environments, synthetic data generation for training.
alpha_potential: Potential application in multi-agent scenarios like algorithmic trading where decentralized execution is needed, but requires significant adaptation from wireless networks to financial markets.

title: Sentinel: Decoding Context Utilization via Attention Probing for Efficient LLM Context Compression
summary: Retrieved contexts are often long, noisy, and redundant, motivating query-aware compression before answer generation. Native attention provides signals for context selection, but heterogeneous head behaviors complicate their direct aggregation into sentence-utility scores. We introduce Sentinel, a sentence-level compressor that learns to combine these signals through a signed linear readout across layers and heads. Only the readout is trained using existing QA evidence annotations, while the backbone remains frozen and sentence scoring requires no autoregressive generation. Across twelve LongBench tasks, Sentinel with a 0.5B backbone outperforms Full Context on multiple tasks under a 2,000-token budget with each of three readers: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. Despite English-only QA supervision, the same readout transfers to Chinese tasks without task-specific retraining. Length-stratified profiling further shows lower compression latency and GPU memory usage than LLMLingua-2 and CPC.
core_methodology: Sentence-level context compression using attention signals from a frozen LLM backbone with a trained linear readout
data_sources: General QA datasets (English and Chinese) from LongBench tasks
alpha_potential: Potential for improving efficiency in processing financial documents/reports, but no direct trading signal extraction demonstrated

title: Statistical Complexity of Soft Bellman Residual Minimization
summary: Offline reinforcement learning and offline inverse reinforcement learning aim to recover near-optimal value functions or reward models from a fixed batch of logged trajectories, yet current practice still struggles to enforce Bellman consistency scalably. Bellman residual minimization (BRM) has emerged as an attractive remedy. While globally convergent gradient-based soft (i.e., entropy-regularized) BRM methods for neural networks have recently been established, their statistical complexity under stochastic gradient descent remains largely unknown. In this paper, we address this theoretical gap for soft BRM. Through a Lyapunov-based analysis under a uniform PL condition in the auxiliary variable, we establish an $\mathcal{O}(1 / n)$ primal argument stability bound up to optimization error and an $\mathcal{O}(1 / n)$ statistical complexity for the soft BRM objective under the stated sampling conditions.
core_methodology: Soft Bellman Residual Minimization with entropy regularization for offline reinforcement learning
data_sources: Fixed batch of logged trajectories (not market-specific)
alpha_potential: Potential for improving value function estimation in model-based trading strategies, but requires significant adaptation to financial markets

title: Implicit Credit Learning for Sparse-Reward Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
summary: When a cooperative team receives feedback only at the end of an episode, a single outcome must guide many agents' earlier actions. Learning a dense team reward helps, but its decomposition does not automatically give each agent a useful policy update. We introduce IMAP, an online method that fits a shared Q/V reward model by comparing completed episodes according to their observed terminal outcomes. Local Q/V residuals provide agent-specific rewards; the same normalized weights combine them for a centralized critic and scale local advantages for decentralized PPO actors. We characterize when these local updates follow the learned team objective. With full returns and frozen reward heads, a sharp bound relates their gradient error to variation in future Q/V compatibility; an exact identity identifies additional continuation terms for general GAE. In experiments with terminal-only feedback, IMAP's local-actor configuration attains the highest reported mean among the compared methods on all nine SMACv2 scenarios and four MAMuJoCo tasks, and on two of three SMACLite scenarios. Controlled relay interventions confirm the predicted changes in actor credit while holding the learned team reward fixed. The gradient result concerns the fitted objective; benchmark returns measure performance on the original task outcomes.
core_methodology: Online method (IMAP) for multi-agent reinforcement learning with sparse rewards, using shared Q/V reward models and local Q/V residuals for agent-specific rewards
data_sources: Not specified (assumed to be synthetic or simulated environments like SMACv2 and MAMuJoCo tasks)
alpha_potential: Potential application in multi-agent trading systems where rewards are sparse, but requires significant adaptation to financial markets

title: Anchors in the Machine: Behavioral and Attributional Evidence of Anchoring Bias in LLMs
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly studied as behavioral subjects (e.g., synthetic participants or users) and decision systems (e.g., LLM-as-a-judge), yet it remains unclear how observed cognitive biases relate to changes in model output probabilities. Anchoring bias, a classic human judgment bias, provides a useful test case. Prior research largely relies on generated responses, leaving distributional effects and input-field contributions less explored. This paper advances the study of anchoring in LLMs through three contributions: (1) a log-probability-based behavioral analysis examining how numerical anchors shift distributions over candidate outputs, using alternative questions and anchor pairs alongside a positive control to reduce reliance on potentially memorized stimuli; (2) exact Banzhaf-value attribution over structured prompt fields to quantify anchor contributions to log-probabilities; and (3) an Anchoring Bias Sensitivity Score (ABSS) integrating behavioral and attributional evidence across six open-source models. Results reveal predominantly positive behavioral anchoring effects, varying substantially across models. Gemma-2B, Phi-2, and Llama-2-7B achieve the highest ABSS rankings, whereas other models exhibit weaker behavioral-attributional alignment despite sometimes showing substantial behavioral shifts. Attributional effects also vary across prompts, indicating that behavioral anchoring does not necessarily imply stronger anchor-field contributions. These findings raise questions about LLM reliability as synthetic participants and potential vulnerabilities to numerical cues in automated evaluation and decision-making. More broadly, the framework connects behavioral science with explainable AI, particularly interpretability, and AI safety, providing a reproducible approach to investigating cognitive-bias-like effects in LLMs.
core_methodology: Log-probability-based behavioral analysis and Banzhaf-value attribution to study anchoring bias in LLMs
data_sources: Behavioral responses from open-source LLMs (Gemma-2B, Phi-2, Llama-2-7B, etc.)
alpha_potential: Limited direct alpha potential, but could inform risk management around LLM-based decision systems in trading

title: Private Sparse Sketches for Linear Regression
summary: Sketching compresses a large dataset into a smaller summary, allowing regression on the sketch to approximate the full-data objective. A sketch released under differential privacy can be reused with any non-private regression solver, any number of times, without further privacy loss. We study private sparse sketches for $\ell_2$ and $\ell_1$ regression. We first prove lower bounds on the noise required by common sparse sketches for both problems when the sketching matrix is public. Since regression on a sketch can be solved without revealing the sketching matrix, we construct sketches whose randomness is kept secret. Hiding how individual records enter the sketch provides an additional source of privacy, allowing less noise for the same privacy guarantee. We prove differential privacy guarantees for both constructions, and experiments on real datasets show improved utility over public-sketch baselines.
core_methodology: Private sparse sketching techniques for linear regression, focusing on differential privacy and noise reduction in sketch construction
data_sources: General datasets (not specifically financial), but methodology could theoretically be applied to financial time series
alpha_potential: Potential for privacy-preserving factor modeling or risk estimation, but no direct trading signal generation demonstrated

title: Monotone Optimisation with Learned Projections
summary: Optimisation algorithms typically assume oracle access to objectives and constraints, yet in many applications these functions are available only through data. To recover them, a common approach learns a surrogate for each function and optimises over it, but this can be unnecessarily expensive and may fail to preserve the structure required by the optimisation algorithm. We study this problem for monotone optimisation, a class of non-convex problems which can be solved globally using the Polyblock Outer Approximation (POA) algorithm. Our key observation is that POA does not require the constraint functions themselves, but only a scalar quantity we call the radial inverse. Learning this quantity directly replaces POA's inner bisection loop over a learned constraint with a single radial inverse evaluation. We characterise exactly which maps arise as radial inverses of monotone constraints, and relate their approximation error to perturbations of the feasible set and optimal objective value. Building on these results, we introduce Homogeneous-Monotone Radial Inverse (HM-RI) networks, structured min-max models that enforce the monotonicity and positive-homogeneity of radial inverses by construction. Across synthetic monotone optimisation problems and a cellular transmit-power application, HM-RI improves solution quality over direct constraint surrogates and local optimisation baselines by up to 58.6 percentage points relative to the Oracle reference objective, while achieving a 3.0-4.7x speed-up over bisection-based POA with learned constraint surrogates, with the largest solution-quality gains occurring in data-limited and piecewise-constant settings.
core_methodology: The paper introduces Homogeneous-Monotone Radial Inverse (HM-RI) networks for solving monotone optimisation problems by learning the radial inverse directly, replacing the need for full constraint surrogate models and inner bisection loops.
data_sources: Synthetic monotone optimisation problems and a cellular transmit-power application.
alpha_potential: The methodology could potentially be adapted for portfolio optimisation problems, but the direct financial applications are not explicitly demonstrated.

title: Sparsity and Out-of-Distribution Generalization
summary: Explaining out-of-distribution generalization has been a central problem in epistemology since Goodman's "grue" puzzle in 1946. Today it's a central problem in machine learning, including AI alignment. Here we propose a principled account of OOD generalization with three main ingredients. First, the world is always presented to experience not as an amorphous mass, but via distinguished features (for example, visual and auditory channels). Second, Occam's Razor favors hypotheses that are "sparse," meaning that they depend on as few features as possible. Third, sparse hypotheses will generalize from a training to a test distribution, provided the two distributions sufficiently overlap on their restrictions to the features that are either actually relevant or hypothesized to be. The two distributions could diverge arbitrarily on other features. We prove a simple theorem that formalizes the above intuitions, generalizing the classic sample complexity bound of Blumer et al. to an OOD context. We then generalize sparse classifiers to subspace juntas, where the ground truth classifier depends solely on a low-dimensional linear subspace of the features.
core_methodology: The paper proposes a theoretical framework for out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization based on the principles of feature sparsity and Occam's Razor. It introduces the concept of sparse classifiers and subspace juntas, which depend on a low-dimensional linear subspace of features.
data_sources: The abstract does not specify any particular data sources, but the methodology is general and could be applied to any dataset with distinguishable features.
alpha_potential: The theoretical insights might help in developing robust predictive models that generalize well across different market regimes, but the paper does not provide direct financial applications or empirical results.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Diffusion LLMs with Entropy-Guided Step Selection and Stepwise Advantages
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has been effective for post-training autoregressive (AR) language models, but extending these methods to diffusion language models (DLMs) is challenging due to intractable sequence-level likelihoods. Existing approaches therefore rely on surrogate likelihoods or heuristic approximations, which can introduce bias and obscure the sequential structure of denoising. We formulate diffusion-based sequence generation as a finite-horizon Markov decision process over the denoising trajectory and derive an exact, unbiased policy gradient that decomposes over denoising steps and is expressed in terms of intermediate advantages, without requiring explicit evaluation of the sequence likelihood. To obtain a practical and compute-efficient estimator, we (i) select denoising steps for policy updates via an entropy-guided approximation bound, and (ii) estimate intermediate advantages using a one-step denoising reward naturally provided by the diffusion model, avoiding costly multi-step rollouts. Experiments on coding and logical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art results, with strong competitive performance on mathematical reasoning, outperforming existing RL post-training approaches for DLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/vishnutez/egspo-dllm-rl.
core_methodology: Reinforcement learning applied to diffusion language models with entropy-guided step selection and stepwise advantages
data_sources: Not explicitly financial; used on coding and logical reasoning benchmarks
alpha_potential: Theoretical potential for natural language processing tasks in finance, but no direct trading application demonstrated

title: EvoAgent: An Evolvable Agent Framework with Skill Learning and Multi-Agent Delegation
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on reusable skills, but skills are usually written by hand, and letting an agent change them on its own calls for explicit user control. We report on EvoAgent, an evolvable agent framework built for a foreign trade assistant, and share the engineering choices behind it. We organize the agent as a harness of four components (reasoning, context engineering, tools and state) and confine self-improvement to the user's persistent state: profile, memory and skills. Skills are multi-file packages with lazily loaded references, matched in three stages (keyword, embedding, LLM). The main agent can delegate to sub-agents with their own context, and long histories are compressed while an index of recoverable resources is kept. An offline loop reviews completed sessions to update the profile and memory and to propose skills; in the open-source release a skill changes only after the user confirms the proposal. On 172 foreign trade test cases scored by an LLM judge on five dimensions, GPT-5.2 with EvoAgent scored about 28% higher than GPT-5.2 called directly with only the final query. This is a single run judged by the model under test, so it measures the harness as a whole rather than any one mechanism, and swapping in GPT-4.1 or Qwen3.5-35B-A3B lowered the scores relative to calling those models directly. Several mechanisms described here were added after the version we evaluated and are not evaluated. The evaluation data is proprietary, so the results are for reference only. An open-source release of the code, which is not the evaluated business version, is available at https://github.com/Focus-AI-Center/Mentarc-EvoAgent
core_methodology: An evolvable agent framework with skill learning and multi-agent delegation, focusing on improving LLM agent capabilities through user-controlled skill updates and delegation mechanisms.
data_sources: Proprietary foreign trade test cases, scored by an LLM judge (specific data not disclosed).
alpha_potential: Limited direct applicability to quant trading; potential in automating certain aspects of trade documentation or negotiation processes in foreign trade contexts, but not directly applicable to market alpha generation.

title: Partition-of-Unity Gaussian Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
summary: Gaussian basis functions provide an efficient and flexible alternative to spline activations in Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (KANs), but their performance is sensitive to the Gaussian scale parameter \epsilon. We introduce the partition-of-unity Gaussian KAN (PU-GKAN), a kernel-based normalization framework that transfers the Shepard partition-of-unity principle to trainable KAN edge functions. Each Gaussian edge basis is normalized by its local sum over fixed centers, preserving the standard edge-based architecture and essentially the same trainable coefficient structure as GKAN. The resulting feature map reproduces constants exactly at the edge level and admits an explicit normalized finite-feature kernel interpretation. Numerical experiments show that PU-GKAN reduces sensitivity to \epsilon, improves validation accuracy for most smooth and moderately non-smooth targets, and provides more stable training behavior. These benefits persist across variations in sample size and number of centers, higher-dimensional architectures, and Matern RBF bases. PU-GKAN also improves physics-informed neural networks for Helmholtz and wave equations, with validation-error reductions of up to 90%. These results establish partition-of-unity normalization as a mathematically grounded and broadly applicable framework for improving the reliability and accuracy of radial basis function KANs.
core_methodology: Partition-of-unity Gaussian Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (PU-GKAN) with kernel-based normalization framework for improving radial basis function networks
data_sources: Not specified (likely synthetic data for numerical experiments)
alpha_potential: Potential for improving non-linear function approximation in financial models, but no direct trading application demonstrated

title: Learning a Unified Cross-Model Semantic Dictionary via Gated Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders
summary: Foundation models pretrained on similar data distributions tend to learn overlapping semantic structure, but their representations are distinct due to different model architecture, pretraining objectives and protocols. This prevents unified interpretability and cross-model feature reuse. Existing approaches extract interpretable concepts from individual models and align these concepts in a shared coordinate system using cross-reconstruction objectives, but the alignment only applies to latent coordinates while the concepts themselves remain model-specific and cannot be shared or reused. This paper introduces the Gated Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoder (GB-SAE), which casts unified cross-model interpretability as a representation factorization problem and solves it by simultaneously learning a unified shared dictionary and multiple private model-specific dictionaries via a gated bottleneck sparse autoencoder framework. The shared dictionary encodes the cross-model common semantic structure in unified concepts that are reusable across all participating models (and beyond), while each private dictionary comprises residual concepts that capture model-specific biases. We evaluate GB-SAE with distinct foundation models including ViT, SigLIP, DINOv2, and ConvNeXt. GB-SAE demonstrates superior reconstruction capability, unified and faithful interpretability, strong reusability and generalization to unseen models and downstream tasks. The code is available at https://github.com/trustAIoT/GB-SAE_NeurIPS.
core_methodology: Gated Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoder (GB-SAE) for learning unified and model-specific semantic dictionaries across different foundation models
data_sources: Foundation models including ViT, SigLIP, DINOv2, and ConvNeXt (not financial data)
alpha_potential: Potential for cross-model feature reuse and interpretability, but not directly applicable to financial data or trading strategies

title: JUBILEE: A Benchmark Environment for Off-Policy Evaluation in Debt Collections
summary: Off-policy evaluation (OPE) estimates the value a candidate decision policy would achieve, using only data logged by the policy already in production. In debt collections, unrecorded factors can influence both actions and outcomes. This paper presents JUBILEE, a benchmark environment built around a debt-collections simulator that generates million-loan panels with competing risks, rare recovery events, and hidden factors driving both outcomes and assignment. The evaluation includes an 80-run comparison of tabular and gradient-boosted estimators under two synthetic outcome mechanisms and a 190-run parameter grid. Independent policy simulations provide reference values with estimated Monte Carlo uncertainty for a synthetic reward score and for simulated cash. With hidden factors influencing action assignment, several tabular methods agree closely while underestimating the field-visit policy's score, an error that also appears with boosted models. Intervals from tabular doubly robust estimation usually contain the reference without hidden assignment dependence but mostly miss it when that dependence is present. Estimates from randomized decisions do not show the same large error, although their limited precision leaves policy choice uncertain. The decision consequences depend on how policy value is defined. The field-visit policy ranks last under the score and first under simulated cash, which excludes channel costs. Under cash, log-based estimators miss this best candidate in nearly every run with hidden assignment dependence in the paired study. JUBILEE supports reproducible study of these failure modes under specified collections mechanisms.
core_methodology: Off-policy evaluation (OPE) using tabular and gradient-boosted estimators in a debt-collections simulator
data_sources: Synthetic data generated by a debt-collections simulator with million-loan panels, competing risks, and hidden factors
alpha_potential: Limited direct applicability to trading; focuses on debt collections policy evaluation rather than financial markets

title: Differentiable Agent-Based Modeling for Multi-Echelon Supply Chains: Gradient-Based Optimization of Heterogeneous Policies at Scale
summary: Global supply chains rely on the interactions of thousands of heterogeneous agents, posing significant challenges for optimization. While traditional optimization often assumes homogeneity to ensure tractability, Reinforcement Learning struggles with sample inefficiency when scaling to high-dimensional state spaces. We propose a Differentiable Agent-Based Model for multi-echelon inventory management. By implementing stochastic dynamics via differentiable tensor operations, we enable direct gradient propagation through the simulation. We validate the framework by recovering theoretical Newsvendor optima without supervision. Crucially, we demonstrate ``Mass Personalization'' by optimizing 10,000 distinct agent policies simultaneously in seconds, achieving a 53% cost reduction compared to scalar baselines. Furthermore, we utilize gradient sensitivity analysis to generate causal heatmaps, accurately recovering inherent lead-time delays from the computation graph. This approach bridges the gap between simulation and optimization, enabling the efficient training of self-correcting Digital Twins.
core_methodology: Differentiable Agent-Based Modeling for optimizing heterogeneous agent policies in supply chains
data_sources: Simulated multi-echelon inventory management scenarios
alpha_potential: Limited direct application to financial markets; potential indirect utility for supply chain-related financial instruments

title: Full Fine-Tuning is not the Problem: Why Adam Fails and SGD Succeeds in Few-Shot CLIP Adaptation
summary: Few-shot CLIP adaptation is often treated as a parameterization problem. Full fine-tuning is assumed to overfit, so parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods are preferred. In this paper, we show that this conclusion conflates parameterization with optimization. Across 11 datasets, 3 CLIP backbones, and 5 shot levels, dense full fine-tuning with plain SGD outperforms representative PEFT methods under the reported evaluation protocol, whereas Adam/AdamW collapses. We trace this collapse to unreliable support-set preconditioning. The few-shot second moment systematically underestimates the corresponding full-data statistic, already at initialization. Adam's inverse-square-root normalization converts this error into an oversized adaptive update. Matching Adam's first-step update budget to SGD resolves most of the collapse, whereas numerator-side alignment does not explain the failure. Shampoo and SOAP also fail, so richer preconditioning alone does not resolve the problem. Theory formalizes how few-shot estimation error is amplified into unsafe updates. SGD succeeds because it avoids unreliable preconditioners and stays close to pretrained CLIP. Interpolation probes show low-loss connections along tested directions, and curvature probes show favorable directional curvature. These results identify optimizer-induced preconditioning, not dense full fine-tuning itself, as the main source of failure in few-shot CLIP adaptation.
core_methodology: Comparison of optimization methods (SGD vs Adam/AdamW) in few-shot learning for CLIP adaptation
data_sources: 11 datasets from computer vision domain, not financial data
alpha_potential: Indirect relevance: may inform better model training approaches for financial applications, but no direct trading implementation

title: An Adaptive, Context-Aware, and Stacked Attention Network-Based Recommendation System to Capture Users' Temporal Preference
summary: Recommendation systems have become more important since the widespread use of the Internet. The large amount of information means that it is difficult for users to discover they really need. However, users' preferences can change over time because of the age and the impact of social networks. Recommendation systems must capture users' preferences and recommend suitable items, which is a difficult challenge. This study proposes a novel recommendation system that adapts to the changing preferences of users. By learning and adapting to users' changing preferences better recommendations are provided. This study uses context factors as additional information to model users' preferences more precisely. For the proposed recommendation system, the context is based on users' interaction items within each defined time interval. This study proposes two novel attention mechanisms for the recommendation system. The contextual item attention module captures contextual information, changing pattern in users' preference and the importance of items. The multi-head attention module extends the diversity of users' preferences and adapts to changing preferences. The recommendation performance is improved using additional item's temporal information to model the contextual item's representation. Experiments compare the proposed algorithm with several state-of-the-art recommendation methods using three real-world datasets. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed context-aware recommendation model outperforms traditional methods and demonstrate the effectiveness with which contextual information is captured by the attention mechanism.
core_methodology: The paper proposes a recommendation system using adaptive, context-aware, and stacked attention networks to capture users' temporal preferences.
data_sources: Three real-world datasets (unspecified, but likely from e-commerce or social media platforms).
alpha_potential: Limited direct application to trading; potential indirect value in modeling temporal patterns in user behavior, which could be adapted for investor sentiment analysis.

title: Daily Emergency Call Volume Forecasting using Univariate and Multivariate TimeGPT
summary: This study investigates the potential of TimeGPT, a pretrained foundation model for timeseries, for forecasting daily emergency call volumes. Real-world emergency call data, comprising 2,101 daily observations, are used to evaluate both univariate and multivariate forecasting settings under one-step-ahead and seven-day multi-step-ahead scenarios. The multivariate forecasting incorporates temporal, meteorological, demographic, and socioeconomic variables. A chronological training, validation, and test split is adopted to prevent information leakage, while hyperparameters are selected using the validation set through grid search and early stopping when applicable. Forecasting performance is evaluated using multiple error metrics. Its forecasting performance is compared with several established forecasting approaches, including Seasonal Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average with Exogenous Regressors (SARIMAX), Poisson regression (PR), Negative Binomial regression (NBR), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM). The results show that SARIMAX achieves the best overall performance in the univariate setting. In the multivariate setting, NBR and PR provide best performance. These findings indicate that the large-scale pretraining of TimeGPT do not necessarily translate into superior forecasting accuracy for emergency call volumes. Frugal methods trained solely on the available data remain better for this application.
core_methodology: Evaluation of TimeGPT for time series forecasting compared to traditional methods like SARIMAX, Poisson regression, and machine learning models.
data_sources: Emergency call data with temporal, meteorological, demographic, and socioeconomic variables.
alpha_potential: Limited direct applicability to trading; potential insights into multivariate time series forecasting techniques.

title: DeFSM: Robust and Efficient Decentralization of Federated Submodular Maximization
summary: Submodular maximization seeks a small subset best representing a large dataset. In its federated setting, the server is a single point of failure and some clients may be Byzantine. Removing the server raises a trilemma of decentraliza- tion, efficiency, and security. We propose DeFSM, a Byzantine-robust and communication-efficient architecture that replaces the server with a lightweight smart contract and a pool of independent, consensus-free agents. Its aggregation rule, SafeGM, builds on two notions from combinatorial geometry: Tukey depth and safe points (the points lying in the convex hull of the good points wherever the bad points are). SafeGM makes the robust decision on 2D Gaussian random projections, which the contract can compute efficiently, and lifts it back as a convex combination of actual updates. Since lifting loses information, it uses the projected geometric median only when its depth certifies it, and otherwise a Tukey median. The share of bad updates is then bounded only by a count: how many there are, not what they contain. We prove, and confirm empirically, that this bound controls the solution quality. On CIFAR10 and PathMNIST, with up to 30% Byzantine clients and agents, DeFSM never collapses and retains on average about 91% of the quality of the ideal reference, the geometric median at a trusted central server. The geometric median decentralized in its best setting would retain about 96%, but the contract cannot compute it, and so each agent would have to download six times more data, or each client twice as much.
core_methodology: Byzantine-robust decentralized federated learning for submodular maximization using combinatorial geometry concepts (Tukey depth and safe points) and Gaussian random projections
data_sources: CIFAR10 and PathMNIST datasets (computer vision benchmarks)
alpha_potential: Limited direct applicability - methodology could theoretically be adapted for decentralized portfolio optimization but paper focuses on non-financial datasets

title: AutoQS: Automated Quantization Strategy Design with Large Language Models
summary: Quantization reduces LLM deployment costs, but effective strategies must balance model quality and storage. LLM-driven search can automate strategy design through repeated proposal and evaluation. This process must identify useful strategies within a limited evaluation budget. The key challenge is that \textit{actual quantization is expensive, while inexpensive proxies may not reflect quantized-model performance.} To address this challenge, we present AutoQS, an \textbf{Auto}mated \textbf{Q}uantization \textbf{S}trategy Design with LLMs. AutoQS keeps weight precision fixed and searches group-size allocations across layers and operators under deployment constraints. Evaluation history guides coordinated LLM proposals, while deterministic validation ensures compatible allocations. An inexpensive quality proxy evaluates candidates, and an candidate repository retains alternative allocations to inform subsequent proposals. Periodic actual quantization complements these proxy evaluations with measured quality and checkpoint storage, providing feedback for further search within the evaluation budget. Experiments on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct show that AutoQS improves seven-task average accuracy over uniform-group GPTQ and AWQ by 0.70 and 1.12 percentage points, respectively, at four-bit weight precision.
core_methodology: LLM-driven automated quantization strategy design with proxy evaluations and periodic actual quantization feedback
data_sources: Model weights and performance metrics on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
alpha_potential: Potential for optimizing trading model deployment efficiency, but limited direct trading signal generation

title: FocusBranch: Combinatorial Branch-and-Bound for $\ell_0$ Neural Network Robustness Verification
summary: Verifying the local robustness of neural networks under $\ell_0$ perturbations is inherently combinatorial, as it must reason over all sparse subsets of $\epsilon$ perturbed pixels. This paper presents FocusBranch, a combinatorial branch-and-bound framework for $\ell_0$ robustness verification. The key insight is to make the $\ell_0$-ball decomposable and branchable using a node abstraction, which consists of a focus pixel set $\mathcal{S}$ and a level $l$, permitting at most $\epsilon-l$ pixels outside $\mathcal{S}$. This abstraction unifies two branching mechanisms: concrete nodes branch through upper shadows to fix additional perturbed locations, while super nodes branch through covering designs to cover many perturbation cases with fewer child nodes. FocusBranch proves node safety by concretizing linear relaxations over node-constrained $\ell_0$-balls and recursively branches on unknown nodes. Rather than relying on a fixed verification plan, it samples nodes across levels to estimate safe rates and costs, then selects a starting level and branching strategy predicted to minimize verification time. Experiments on fully connected and convolutional classifiers for MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 show that FocusBranch verifies $\ell_0$ robustness effectively across architectures and outperforms state-of-the-art verifiers. The code is available at: https://github.com/simpl-group/FocusBranch.
core_methodology: Combinatorial branch-and-bound framework for verifying neural network robustness under sparse perturbations
data_sources: Standard image datasets (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10)
alpha_potential: Limited direct applicability - methodology could potentially be adapted for verifying robustness of financial prediction models, but no direct trading application demonstrated

title: Transactional Data Change for Real-Time Analytics in Lakehouses
summary: Real-time data analytics has become a key demand for lakehouses. It requires propagating data changes from the data source to the lakehouse in real time, while ensuring ACID guarantees and minimizing resource consumption and impact on analytical query performance. This is highly challenging for a data system according to the RUM conjecture, especially given the read-optimized immutable file storage layer in lakehouses. Existing lakehouses offer only git-style catalog version control on a single table, and they trade data freshness, query performance, and/or resource efficiency to achieve a barely acceptable data-change throughput. In this paper, we propose a novel data synchronization framework, Retina, that enables real-time, cost-efficient, query-performant, and fully transactional data changes in lakehouses. We implement and open-source Retina. Evaluations show that Retina delivers 10-millisecond-level data freshness and over 3.2 million row/s linear-scalable data-change throughput with low resource consumption and query-performance overhead, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art lakehouse systems and lake-compatible HTAP databases.
core_methodology: Real-time data synchronization framework for lakehouses
data_sources: Transactional data changes in data lake environments
alpha_potential: Potential for faster access to updated market data, but no direct trading signal generation

title: Tensor Network Kernel Machines for Nonlinear System Identification
summary: Over the past ten years Tensor Network Kernel Machines have enabled efficient nonlinear system identification through the use of low-rank tensor networks. The goal of this article is to provide the reader with a basic understanding of this model class in terms of its two defining properties. Furthermore, both the optimization and regularization of such models are discussed, together with recent developments and starting points for further exploration.
core_methodology: Uses low-rank tensor networks for nonlinear system identification
data_sources: Not specified (likely general time-series data)
alpha_potential: Potential for modeling complex nonlinear relationships in financial time series, but no direct trading application demonstrated

title: Agnostic Marginal-Nonuniform Learning
summary: We study the problem of binary classification in the marginal-nonuniform learning framework in the agnostic setting. In this model, the constants in the learning rate may depend on the marginal distribution of the unlabeled data, but the guarantee must hold uniformly over all conditional distributions of the labels. We also study fine-grained rates. We consider two criteria. (1) The standard agnostic setting, where the learner competes with the best concept in the class. In this setting, an immediate consequence of standard agnostic PAC learning results gives us the optimal rate of $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$ for every class $\mathcal{H}$ with finite $\mathrm{VC}(\mathcal{H})$ and shows that arbitrarily slow rates are necessary otherwise. This also gives us the optimal fine-grained rate of $\sqrt{\tfrac{\mathrm{VC}(\mathcal{H})}{n}}$. Therefore, the dependence on the marginal distribution does not help, which is in contrast to the realizable setting. (2) In the relaxed agnostic setting, where the learner competes with $(1+\lambda)$ times the error of the best concept for a fixed $\lambda \in (0,1]$, the picture from the realizable setting reappears. We obtain a trichotomy of the achievable optimal rates: exponential rates of the form $e^{-n}$ arise precisely when the class is finite; linear rates of the form $\tfrac{1}{n}$ arise when the class is infinite but $\mathrm{VC}(\mathcal{H})$ is finite; and arbitrarily slow rates occur when $\mathrm{VC}(\mathcal{H})=\infty$. We also obtain the optimal fine-grained rate of $\tfrac{\mathrm{uVCE}(\mathcal{H})}{\lambda n}$, where $\mathrm{uVCE}(\mathcal{H})$ is a recently introduced combinatorial complexity dimension called the uncentered $\mathrm{VC}$-eluder dimension.
core_methodology: Binary classification in the marginal-nonuniform learning framework, focusing on agnostic learning rates and fine-grained analysis of VC dimensions.
data_sources: Theoretical framework, no specific financial data mentioned.
alpha_potential: Limited direct application to trading; potential theoretical foundation for classification tasks in finance but requires significant adaptation.

title: Programming Prescience: Issues in Human Construction of Forecasting Bots
summary: AI models' growing capacity for complex reasoning has made them attractive tools for forecasting, or the systematic prediction of the future based on past and present data. However, should AI forecasting systems be adopted, human builders will shoulder the work of building and evaluating them. In this paper, we explore what this work looks like with a qualitative interview study with 15 builders of forecasting bots, sampled from among successful participants in a recent AI forecasting competition. Our analysis surfaces the challenges around (1) tuning a bot to acquire factual research, (2) implementing coherent reasoning, and (3) understanding how well one's bot actually does. During their work, builders frequently introduced complexity that did not pay off, and tested in ways that were opportunistic and piecemeal. Our detailed account of their challenges helps clarify what problems should be targeted in upcoming innovations in process, tools, and human-AI teaming for forecasting.
core_methodology: Qualitative interview study with builders of forecasting bots
data_sources: Interviews with participants from an AI forecasting competition
alpha_potential: Limited direct alpha potential, focuses on human challenges in building forecasting systems rather than specific financial applications

title: ESAA: Event Sourcing for Autonomous Agents in LLM-Based Software Engineering
summary: Autonomous agents based on Large Language Models (LLMs) have evolved from reactive assistants to systems capable of planning, executing actions via tools, and iterating over environment observations. However, they remain vulnerable to structural limitations: lack of native state, context degradation over long horizons, and the gap between probabilistic generation and deterministic execution requirements. This paper presents the ESAA (Event Sourcing for Autonomous Agents) architecture, which separates the agent's cognitive intention from the project's state mutation, inspired by the Event Sourcing pattern. In ESAA, agents emit only structured intentions in validated JSON (agent.result or issue.report); a deterministic orchestrator validates, persists events in an append-only log (activity.jsonl), applies file-writing effects, and projects a verifiable materialized view (roadmap.json). The proposal incorporates boundary contracts (AGENT_CONTRACT.yaml), metaprompting profiles (PARCER), and replay verification with hashing (esaa verify), ensuring the immutability of completed tasks and forensic traceability. Two case studies validate the architecture: (i) a landing page project (9 tasks, 49 events, single-agent composition) and (ii) a clinical dashboard system (50 tasks, 86 events, 4 concurrent agents across 8 phases), both concluding with run.status=success and verify_status=ok. The multi-agent case study demonstrates real concurrent orchestration with heterogeneous LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Codex GPT-5, Antigravity/Gemini 3 Pro, and Claude Opus 4.6), providing empirical evidence of the architecture's scalability beyond single-agent scenarios.
core_methodology: Event Sourcing architecture for autonomous agents in software engineering, focusing on structured intention emission and deterministic orchestration
data_sources: Not applicable (software engineering projects)
alpha_potential: Limited direct application to trading; potential conceptual relevance for multi-agent systems in market simulation

title: Memory flows: geometry and dynamics of sequential retrieval in input-driven Hopfield networks
summary: Associative memory models classically describe retrieval as convergence to stored patterns, but the theory of sequential retrieval remains comparatively limited. We develop a two-timescale input-driven Hopfield network in which fast associative retrieval is modulated by a slow feedback variable evolving over a prescribed memory-transition graph. This yields autonomous, graph-constrained transitions while preserving analytical tractability. Using slow-fast and geometric singular perturbation theory, we characterize memory fixation via memory manifolds and identify the geometric regions that govern stability loss and escape from retrieved memories. We further derive reduced slow dynamics and explicit criteria for transition onset, self-sustained retrieval, and collapse, expressed through escape times, gain thresholds, and fixed points. Together, these results provide a tractable framework for analyzing feedback-driven sequential retrieval in Hopfield networks.
core_methodology: Two-timescale input-driven Hopfield network with slow feedback for sequential memory retrieval
data_sources: Theoretical model, no specific financial data mentioned
alpha_potential: Potential theoretical framework for modeling sequential patterns in financial time series, but no direct trading application demonstrated

title: Adaptive Budgeted Data Acquisition for Robust Off-Policy Evaluation from Multiple Loggers
summary: We consider off-policy evaluation when additional data can be purchased from several existing logging policies (or loggers) with heterogeneous costs per observation. While existing work on multiple loggers presumes a fixed number of observations from each logger, we study how to allocate a limited budget across them sequentially to evaluate a finite class of target policies. We propose Adaptive Greedy, an algorithm that purchases observations sequentially from the affordable logger that has the most cost-normalized variance reduction across the target policies. It turns out that each such purchase is an 'approximate conditional-gradient step' for the corresponding design problem. Under mild assumptions, we establish that the empirical allocation converges almost surely to the optimal design at an explicit rate. We also derive the asymptotic normality of the final pooled estimator and show that it attains the semiparametric efficiency bound. Simulations and a semi-synthetic application based on the AIDS Clinical Trials Group Study 175 show that Adaptive Greedy outperforms standard allocation strategies, remains accurate if stopped early, and matches the final accuracy of repeated integer programming at a fraction of its computational cost.
core_methodology: Sequential budget allocation algorithm for off-policy evaluation using multiple heterogeneous data loggers
data_sources: Simulated data and semi-synthetic data from AIDS Clinical Trials Group Study
alpha_potential: Limited direct alpha potential, primarily focused on experimental design for policy evaluation rather than financial markets

title: Learning calibrated probabilistic forecasts using Koopman mode decomposition and the continuous ranked probability score
summary: Well-calibrated forecasting for non-linear dynamical systems is essential in science and engineering applications such as fluid dynamics and weather prediction. We present a forecasting method combining probabilistic machine learning with the structured linear dynamics of Koopman mode decomposition. Within this framework, the observation, linear dynamics, and state reconstruction operators are constructed using standard machine learning architectures, producing predictive distributions via the pushforward of injected noise samples. The model is trained using a proper scoring rule, the continuous ranked probability score, to directly target calibrated, accurate forecasts. The approach is validated on two non-linear ordinary differential equation examples and two partial differential equation examples, vortex shedding and cavity flow, using both large and small, noisy datasets. Results demonstrate that known Koopman eigenfunctions and spectra can be identified and used for accurate forecasting. The model can also produce multi-modal predictive distributions, demonstrated for a trajectory initialised on the boundary between two basins of attraction. Uncertainty is captured by the sample ensemble spread, with spread--skill ratios close to one over the training horizon in several experiments, although for extended rollouts and noisy datasets, the ensemble may become under- or over-dispersed. In low-noise experiments, temporal rollout is generally accurate for at least twice the training horizon, and up to twenty times in some cases. Approximation quality is comparable to a deep ensemble approximation over the training horizon, but at a reduced computational cost and with better robustness in identifying Koopman eigenvalues.
core_methodology: Combines probabilistic machine learning with Koopman mode decomposition for forecasting non-linear dynamical systems, focusing on calibration and uncertainty quantification using the continuous ranked probability score.
data_sources: Simulated data from non-linear ordinary differential equations, partial differential equations (vortex shedding and cavity flow), including both large and small, noisy datasets.
alpha_potential: Limited direct application to financial markets; potential indirect value in modeling complex market dynamics or regime shifts, but requires significant adaptation.

title: The balance between feature learning and collapse in dynamical systems-based generative models
summary: Over the past decade, a growing body of work has established that implicit biases in learning dynamics fundamentally shape the solutions found by neural networks, governing their learned features and generalisation performance. However, despite these strides in deep learning theory, far less is known about representation learning in generative models based on dynamical systems, from normalising flows to diffusion. Importantly, empirical evidence suggests that continuous-time generative models can be prone to mode collapse, yet a learning theory explaining such biases remains elusive. To address this, we use tools from dynamical systems and operator theory to express the gradient flow of a general class of stochastic differential equations as a composition of linear operators, allowing us to relate collapse to low-rank biases in generative models. In variational inference and flow-matching tasks, we show that this bias can manifest in two different mechanisms: i) where collapsed models are stable fixed points of the gradient flow, or ii) in sequential feature learning, where smaller modes take progressively longer to be learned, producing an effective collapse for a fixed training budget. Together these findings point to a trade-off between feature learning and collapse, suggesting an operator view as a step towards a unified framework for understanding the learning dynamics of dynamical systems-based generative models.
core_methodology: Analysis of gradient flow in dynamical systems-based generative models using tools from dynamical systems and operator theory
data_sources: Not specified (theoretical study)
alpha_potential: Limited direct applicability; potential insights into generative model behavior that could inform synthetic data generation for trading strategies

title: Graph and Simplicial Complex Prediction Gaussian Process via the Hodgelet Representations
summary: Predicting labels for graph-structured data is crucial in many scientific applications. Recently, Gaussian processes with graph-level inputs have been proposed as flexible non-parametric models for classification tasks. In this work, we extend this framework to regression tasks and to simplicial complexes, enabling the modelling of attributes defined on edges and higher-order simplices. Drawing on Hodge theory, we construct representations based on the Hodge decomposition, allowing the model to distinguish between exact, co-exact, and harmonic signal components. We introduce Hodgelet representations as rich, learnable topological descriptors of simplicial complexes and show that our framework improves predictive performance across a range of applications. Our work broadens the applicability of Gaussian processes to prediction tasks at the graph and simplicial-complex levels.
core_methodology: Gaussian processes with Hodge decomposition for graph and simplicial complex data
data_sources: Graph-structured data and simplicial complexes (could theoretically include financial networks or correlation structures)
alpha_potential: Potential for analyzing complex relational data structures in finance, though practical trading applications would require significant adaptation

title: RAPTOR: Ridge-Adaptive Logistic Probes
summary: Probing studies what information is encoded in a frozen LLM's layer representations by training a lightweight predictor on top of them. Beyond analysis, probes are often used operationally in probe-then-steer pipelines: a learned concept vector is extracted from a probe and injected via additive activation steering by adding it to a layer representation during the forward pass. The effectiveness of this pipeline hinges on estimating concept vectors that are accurate, directionally stable under ablation, and inexpensive to obtain. Motivated by these desiderata, we propose RAPTOR (Ridge-Adaptive Logistic Probe), a simple L2-regularized logistic probe whose validation-tuned ridge strength yields concept vectors from normalized weights. Across extensive experiments on instruction-tuned LLMs and human-written concept datasets, RAPTOR matches or exceeds strong baselines in accuracy while achieving competitive directional stability and substantially lower training cost; these quantitative results are supported by qualitative downstream steering demonstrations. Finally, using the Convex Gaussian Min-max Theorem (CGMT), we provide a mechanistic characterization of ridge logistic regression in an idealized Gaussian teacher-student model in the high-dimensional few-shot regime, explaining how penalty strength mediates probe accuracy and concept-vector stability and yielding structural predictions that qualitatively align with trends observed on real LLM embeddings.
core_methodology: L2-regularized logistic probe for extracting concept vectors from LLM layer representations
data_sources: Human-written concept datasets on instruction-tuned LLMs
alpha_potential: Potential for extracting financial sentiment or concept vectors from LLMs, but not directly applied to market data

title: SHERLOC: Statistical Hypothesis Evaluation and Recovery for Learning Opponent Characteristics
summary: When used in automated decision-making systems, machine learning (ML) models are vulnerable to data-manipulation attacks. Some defense mechanisms (e.g., adversarial regularization) directly affect the ML models while others (e.g., anomaly detection) act within the broader system. However, many defenses operate under a predefined threat model that assumes characteristics of the adversary, including their knowledge, capabilities, and objectives, are known and fixed. In practice, these characteristics may be unknown or evolve over time, creating a mismatch between the assumptions of the defender and the true attacker. In this paper, we study a new perspective on adversarial defense: focusing on the attacker, rather than the attack. We present and demonstrate SHERLOC, a framework for adversarial learning forensics -- namely, a detective that learns about the attacker from observed attack(s). We prove that, without additional knowledge, the attacker is non-identifiable --- multiple potential attackers would perform the same observed attack. This reveals an important distinction between reconstructing an attacker's behavior and recovering the attacker that generated it. We demonstrate empirically that SHERLOC is able to reconstruct a hypothesis attacker that is consistent with the observed attacks against various defender models (i.e., generalized least-squares linear regressors, logistic regressors, and polynomial classifiers) across various security-critical domains. Finally, we show that these inferred attackers need not match the ground truth attacker exactly to have downstream utility. Defenses using the SHERLOC-inferred attackers achieve approximately 90-100% of robustness improvement that would be achieved if the defender had access to the ground-truth attacker.
core_methodology: Learning opponent characteristics through adversarial learning forensics
data_sources: Observed attacks or adversarial inputs
alpha_potential: Limited direct application to quantitative trading; potential indirect application in improving robustness of trading models against adversarial attacks

title: Learning inexact alternating minimization for convex problems with quadratic coupling
summary: Alternating minimization is a standard tool for optimization problems with two coupled variable blocks. Its cost is dominated by the inner subproblem solvers, which rarely have a closed-form solution. In this paper, we propose to learn an inexact alternating scheme in which neural networks approximate the subproblem solution at each iteration. For convex problems with quadratic couplings between the variable blocks that satisfy a quadratic growth condition, we derive a worst-case bound on the optimality gap that exposes the per-iteration error that each network is trained to minimize in a greedy fashion. Combining the bound with a PAC-Bayes argument, we obtain a fixed-horizon, high-probability bound on the expected optimality gap over the distribution of problem instances. We apply the learned scheme to robust matrix completion and low-dose CT reconstruction with dictionary regularization where we achieve a 5x-13x speedup over the inexact first-order baseline at matched accuracy. A brief end-to-end fine-tuning stage extends this up to 30x and outperforms other learned schemes. The code is available at https://github.com/paulhausner/learned-alternating-minimization.
core_methodology: A neural network-based approach to learn inexact alternating minimization for convex optimization problems with quadratic coupling
data_sources: Dataset not specified, but likely synthetic data or from non-financial domains like robust matrix completion and CT reconstruction
alpha_potential: Low; the paper focuses on general optimization problems without specific applications to financial markets or trading strategies
